When are New London real estate taxes due?

Real estate taxes over $100 are due July 1 and January 1. The city lists the January 1, 2027 installment as last payable without penalty on Monday, February 1, 2027.

Does New London mail the second tax bill?

No. Bills are mailed in June with enough copies for each installment, and the city does not mail second installment bills for real estate. They can be printed from the online tax portal.

How much interest does New London charge on late taxes?

Interest on delinquent taxes accrues at 1.5 percent per month, with a minimum of $2.00 under state statute.

How much is the conveyance tax on a New London house?

For a residential sale up to $800,000 the base combined rate is 1 percent, 0.75 percent state and 0.25 percent municipal. The state rate is higher on the portion above $800,000.

Is New London mostly land or water?

Nearly half the city is water. Of 10.59 square miles total, 5.61 are land and 4.98 are water.

Where is East Haven and how is the town laid out?

East Haven is a shoreline town in New Haven County, about 3 miles east of New Haven, with Long Island Sound on its southern edge. It covers 13.4 square miles, of which 1.2 are water, and the 2020 Census counted 27,923 residents.

On a map the town is taller than it is wide. It borders New Haven on the west, North Haven on the north, and Branford, North Branford and Lake Saltonstall on the east. East Haven shares Tweed New Haven Airport and the Alling Memorial Golf Course with New Haven. It also includes Stony Island, offshore from the town beach.

East Haven is about 35 miles from Hartford and 82 miles from New York City. The Connecticut Colony granted township here in May 1707, replacing the earlier name of Iron Works Village, and the town was incorporated in 1785.

What are the sections of East Haven?

Residents split East Haven into three large sections instead of many small neighborhoods. Each has a different character, and that shows up in buyer questions.

  • Foxon: the hilliest part of town, in the north and east around State Route 80. It holds the high school and Foxon Park Beverage.
  • Momauguin: the southern shore section, with the town beach, condominiums, summer cottages and an industrial park near the airport.
  • The Center: the administrative hub, with Town Hall, the fire department headquarters, Hagaman Memorial Library and the Old Stone Church, built in 1774. It includes the West End, next to New Haven.

A shoreline cottage in Momauguin, a hillside house in Foxon and an older house in the West End will draw very different questions. Tell us the section when you contact us.

East Haven's climate is tempered by Long Island Sound, so winters are milder and snow is lighter than inland, but storms are a real part of owning a shoreline house. The town averages about 27 inches of snow in a normal winter and about 45 inches of precipitation a year.

The town has no hospital. Yale New Haven Hospital and related facilities are 3 to 5 miles away in New Haven, and the town runs the East Haven Public School system and the Hagaman Memorial Library.

Your closing attorney sets the exact amount and the codes. Ask early, because the return goes with the deed.

Where is Wethersfield, and what kind of town is it?

Wethersfield is a Hartford County town that sits immediately south of Hartford along the Connecticut River, in the Capitol Planning Region. It covers about 13.1 square miles, of which roughly 12.3 are land, and the 2020 census counted 27,298 people.

The town was settled in October 1634 and incorporated on February 21, 1637, alongside Windsor and Hartford. That makes it one of the three oldest English settlements in Connecticut, and it still calls itself "Ye Most Ancient Town in Connecticut." The town uses ZIP code 06109, and Route 99, the Silas Deane Highway, runs through it.

For a seller, the age of the town matters more than the nickname. A town with this much 17th, 18th and 19th century building stock will have owners facing roof, electrical or foundation questions before a conventional buyer's inspector signs off.

What is Old Wethersfield, and how does it affect a house sale?

Old Wethersfield is a National Register historic district, added in 1970, that spans about two square miles and holds roughly 1,100 buildings from the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries. It is described as the largest historic district in Connecticut.

Three buildings in town are individually listed as National Register landmarks: the Buttolph-Williams House on Broad Street, the Joseph Webb House at 211 Main Street, and the Silas Deane House at 203 Main Street. The Webb House is where, in May 1781, George Washington and Rochambeau planned the Siege of Yorktown.

If your house is inside the district, expect buyers to ask about its age, its original windows and any prior alterations. Older framing, knob and tube wiring, oil heat and stone foundations are common questions. Outside the district the stock is mostly 20th century, but the same pattern of deferred maintenance applies. Ask the town's building office what permits are on file for your address before you list, because a missing permit for a finished basement or a replaced furnace can stall a conventional closing.

How is Wethersfield laid out, and which roads matter to buyers?

Interstate 91 is the main highway through town, with exits 25 and 26 serving Wethersfield, and several state routes cross it. Hartford sits directly to the north, which is the main reason many buyers look here.

  • Interstate 91, exits 25 to 26
  • Route 99 (Silas Deane Highway), the main commercial spine
  • Route 175 (Wells Road) and Route 287 (Prospect Street)
  • Route 15 and U.S. Route 5 (Berlin Turnpike and Wilbur Cross Highway)
  • Route 3 (Maple Street and the Putnam Bridge)

Public transit is bus based. CT Transit runs routes 43, 47, 53, 55, 61 and 91 through Wethersfield, and Hartford station is the nearest passenger rail stop. The old rail line through town carries occasional freight trains between Hartford and Old Saybrook.

The town's public schools include Wethersfield High School, Silas Deane Middle School and five elementary schools: Highcrest, Charles Wright, Emerson-Williams, Alfred W. Hanmer and Samuel B. Webb. Corpus Christi School is a private Catholic school for pre-kindergarten through eighth grade, and the CREC Discovery Academy is a STEM magnet.

Who employs people in Wethersfield?

State government is the largest employer in Wethersfield, followed by the town itself. According to the town's 2021 annual financial report, as summarized on Wikipedia, the top employers were these.

The state's Department of Correction and Department of Motor Vehicles are headquartered here, and the Department of Labor is based on Folly Brook Boulevard. Public employers with hundreds of workers each give the town a steady job base, and several state agencies keep offices in town.

What are the property tax numbers a Wethersfield seller should know?

The town's assessor lists a mill rate of 39.98 for real estate and personal property on the 2025 Grand List, and 32.46 for motor vehicles. The assessment year runs from October 1 to September 30.

Wethersfield finished a state-mandated revaluation for the October 1, 2024 Grand List, and the Town Council adopted a four-year phase-in of the new values. The assessor's own example shows how it works: a property moving from $200,000 to $300,000 in assessment steps up by $25,000 a year, reaching $225,000, $250,000, $275,000 and then $300,000.

The practical effect for sellers is that a buyer's tax bill will keep rising for the remaining phase-in years even if the mill rate holds steady. Anyone comparing offers should ask the assessor's office for the current phased assessment on the specific parcel.

How does the conveyance tax work when a Wethersfield house closes?

Connecticut charges a real estate conveyance tax when a deed is recorded, and the seller's side files the return. The Department of Revenue Services says the grantor, the grantor's attorney or an authorized agent must file Form OP-236 when the price is $2,000 or more, unless an exemption applies.

The return is filed and the tax paid when the deed is recorded. Wethersfield's town code on the state form is 159. The state also lists an exemption for a principal residence sold for less than the mortgages plus the real estate taxes and municipal liens that rank ahead of them, which matters if you owe more than the house will bring.

Rates and municipal shares change, so confirm them with the town clerk or your closing attorney instead of relying on an old figure.

What do Wethersfield sellers usually run into?

The common situations are older houses with deferred repairs, inherited homes held by several heirs, and owners who are behind on taxes or a mortgage. In a town with this much historic building stock, repair lists can run long.

  • Roof, chimney or window work on a house built before 1900
  • A basement or foundation that has seen water, which matters near the river and the Cove
  • Heirs who live out of state and cannot agree on a list price
  • Tax or lien balances that must be paid from sale proceeds
  • Tenants in a multi-family house who are not cooperative on showings

A cash buyer purchases the house in its current condition, so repairs and showings are off the table. The tradeoff is that the offer reflects the work required. Ask for the offer in writing and compare it with what a listing would net after repairs, concessions and months of carrying costs.

What does the town's history tell you about flood and ground risk?

Wethersfield grew on Connecticut River floodplain, and its history includes the 1936 flood pictured in town records summarized on Wikipedia. The town is also home to Great Meadows along the river and the Wethersfield Cove.

Not every house is affected, but a buyer's lender will normally check flood zone status for riverside and low-lying addresses. Check your parcel's flood zone with the town and FEMA before you decide how to sell.

The area's farming past is also worth knowing. Wethersfield was a center of the New England onion trade, and the seed company founded there in 1820 became America's oldest continuously operating seed company.

Frequently asked questions

How many people live in Wethersfield?

The 2020 census counted 27,298 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate used on this page is 27,291. The town covers about 13.1 square miles south of Hartford.

What is the Wethersfield mill rate?

The town's assessor lists 39.98 for real estate and personal property on the 2025 Grand List and 32.46 for motor vehicles. Confirm the current figure with the Assessor's Office at 860-721-2810 before you rely on it.

Does the 2024 revaluation phase-in affect a buyer's tax bill?

Yes. The Town Council adopted a four-year phase-in, so a property whose assessment rose is stepped up in equal parts each year. A buyer should ask for the phased assessment that applies to the parcel.

Who files the Connecticut conveyance tax return on a sale?

The seller, the seller's attorney or an authorized agent files Form OP-236 when the deed is recorded and the price is $2,000 or more. Wethersfield's town code on the form is 159.

Can I sell a house in Old Wethersfield as is?

Yes. Nothing in the state conveyance rules requires repairs before a sale, though a conventional buyer's lender and inspector may ask for them. A cash buyer can purchase the house in its current condition.

What if I owe more than the house is worth?

Connecticut's conveyance tax has an exemption for a principal residence when the price does not cover the mortgages and priority tax liens. Talk to your closing attorney about how that applies to your sale.

Where is South Windsor, Connecticut, and how is the town laid out?

South Windsor is a town in Hartford County, part of the Capitol Planning Region, on the east bank of the Connecticut River. The Census Bureau count for 2020 was 26,918 residents, and the town covers 28.7 square miles, of which 28.1 is land.

Old Main Street runs north to south near the river from the East Windsor line to the East Hartford line, and it anchors the oldest part of town. Newer subdivisions, shopping areas and industrial parks sit farther east. The town is council-manager run, with a nine-member Town Council that meets at 1540 Sullivan Avenue.

If you own a house here, your neighbors are likely long-term residents. 10,804 housing units and 9,926 households in the 2020 census, so the town has roughly one housing unit for every 2.5 residents.

What is the history behind South Windsor's housing stock?

The area was farmland first. Settlers from Windsor began grazing and farming the east bank in the middle of the 1600s, and South Windsor became its own town in 1845. Tobacco has been a major crop since the start.

The big change came after 1950. The census count rose from 4,066 in 1950 to 9,460 in 1960 and 15,553 in 1970, and it reached 24,412 by 2000. Most of the houses built in that wave are now 50 to 70 years old, which is the age when roofs, boilers, windows and septic or sewer connections tend to need work.

The town also has three entries on the National Register of Historic Places: the East Windsor Hill Historic District, the Elmore Houses on Long Hill Road, and the Windsor Farms Historic District. An owner of an older home near Main Street should ask the town's land use staff what rules apply before planning exterior changes, because historic status can shape what a buyer is allowed to do.

What does South Windsor's climate mean for a house?

South Windsor has cold winters and warm, damp summers. Weather Channel figures quoted by Wikipedia show a January average low of 18 degrees Fahrenheit, a July average high of 84, and about 43.7 inches of precipitation a year, spread fairly evenly across the months.

Those numbers translate into specific wear on a house:

  • Freeze and thaw cycles stress driveways, chimneys, foundations and roof flashing.
  • Record lows of minus 24 degrees mean un-winterized pipes in vacant or inherited houses can burst.
  • Steady rainfall in every month makes basements and crawl spaces a common inspection issue.
  • The Connecticut River and Scantic River border parts of town, so ask your insurer or lender about flood zone status for your parcel.

A vacant house loses value quickly if heat is shut off for a winter. If you are handling an inherited or vacated South Windsor property, keep utilities on and the roof tight until it sells.

How do roads and schools affect who buys a South Windsor house?

South Windsor sits between Hartford and the Massachusetts line, and Wikipedia's historic district listing places U.S. Route 5 and Interstate 291 along the western edge of town near the river. East Hartford borders the town to the south and East Windsor to the north.

Public school students attend one of four elementary schools (Pleasant Valley, Orchard Hill, Philip R. Smith and Eli Terry), then Timothy Edwards Middle School, then South Windsor High School. Wapping Elementary was turned over to the high school in 2023 for classroom space because of growing enrollment. School assignment is a top question for buyers with children, so mention your street's school if you list the house.

The 2020 census data reported by Wikipedia shows a median age of 41.4 and a median household income of $126,996. Buyers in this price range often use conventional financing and ask for repairs after inspection, which is one reason some sellers choose to skip that step.

What does it cost to sell a house in Connecticut?

Connecticut charges a real estate conveyance tax on the seller. State law sets the base rate at three-quarters of one percent to the state plus one-quarter of one percent to the town, on any deed where the consideration is $2,000 or more (Chapter 223, Sec. 12-494).

Higher state rates apply to the part of a residential price above $800,000: 1.25 percent up to $2.5 million and 2.25 percent above that. Non-residential property other than unimproved land pays 1.25 percent to the state.

The seller, the seller's attorney or an authorized agent files Form OP-236 when the deed is recorded, and the tax is due at that moment. The deed goes to the town clerk, whose land records office records it. Ask the South Windsor town clerk whether the town is on the electronic system and what the recording fee is, because both can change.

  • Gather the deed, payoff statements and the buyer's name before the closing date.
  • Ask the title or closing attorney to prepare Form OP-236.
  • Confirm that unpaid property tax and sewer charges are paid from proceeds.
  • Keep copies of the recorded deed and the tax return.

How are property taxes billed on a South Windsor home you are selling?

State law lets each town choose one, two or four installments, and the last installment must fall at least 45 days before the fiscal year ends (Chapter 204, Sec. 12-142). A late installment becomes delinquent and accrues interest at 18 percent a year, with a minimum of $2 per installment unless the town waives it (Sec. 12-146).

Check the exact due dates and the mill rate with the South Windsor Collector of Revenue or the Assessor. Sellers should also ask that office whether any sewer or other municipal charges are open on the parcel.

Yes, a cash purchase can close without a bank appraisal or lender repair demands, so a house with an old roof, a failing septic or sewer connection, or deferred maintenance can still sell. Where is Simsbury, CT, and what is the setting?

Simsbury is a town in Hartford County at the northern end of the Farmington Valley, with a 2020 census population of 24,517. It covers about 34.3 square miles and belongs to the Capitol Planning Region.

The Farmington River runs through town. Talcott Mountain, part of the Metacomet Ridge, flanks the east side, and Heublein Tower, Talcott Mountain State Park, Penwood State Park and the Tariffville Gorge are all along that ridge. The Pinchot Sycamore, the largest tree in Connecticut, grows near the river. Belden Forest, a 40-acre old-growth tract near the town center, joined the Old-Growth Forest Network in 2019.

Homes close to the river, the ridge and the state parks draw their own kinds of buyers.

What is Simsbury's history?

Simsbury was incorporated on May 12, 1670, as Connecticut's 21st town, on land the Massaco band had lived on. Settlers from Windsor came in the 1660s.

In March 1676, during King Philip's War, the town was pillaged and burned, and settlers stayed in Windsor until spring 1677. The area later split into Granby in 1786 and Canton in 1806. On December 20, 1859, the Patent Safety Fuse factory near the town center exploded and killed eight people. Ensign-Bickford, founded in Simsbury in 1836, is still headquartered in town.

The population was 4,822 in 1950 and 10,138 in 1960, then 17,475 in 1970. Much of the housing came with that postwar jump, with older homes in the historic districts.

Which Simsbury villages and districts matter to a seller?

Simsbury has four census-designated places: Simsbury Center, Tariffville, Weatogue and West Simsbury. Early resettled communities were East Weatogue, Simsbury Center and Terry's Plain.

The terrain is hilly and rocky. Elevation runs from about 342 feet at Branchville to 1,060 feet at Pine Mountain, and glaciers left rocks scattered across the landscape. Public open space totals roughly 5,200 acres, about 23 percent of the town.

Those hills affect a house. Driveway grade and drainage are details Ridgefield buyers and inspectors will ask about.

How did Ridgefield develop?

Ridgefield was settled in 1708 by English colonists from Norwalk who bought the land from Chief Catoonah, and it was incorporated in 1709. For most of its history it was farm country.

The Battle of Ridgefield took place on April 27, 1777, when colonial forces under General David Wooster and Benedict Arnold met a British force returning from a raid on Danbury. The Keeler Tavern, still standing at 132 Main Street, has a British cannonball lodged in its side.

In the late nineteenth century the railroad connection and cooler hill elevation drew wealthy New Yorkers, who built large estates. After the Great Depression many of those estates were broken up, and subdivisions of one- and two-acre lots turned the town into a commuter suburb in the 1950s through the 1970s. The population rose from 4,356 in 1950 to 18,188 in 1970.

The Lounsbury House at 316 Main Street, built around 1896 by Governor Phineas Chapman Lounsbury, is now the Ridgefield Veterans Memorial Community Center. Other National Register listings include the Benedict House and Shop on Rockwell Road, the Lewis June House on North Salem Road and the Thomas Hyatt House on Barlow Mountain Road.

The result is a mix of historic village houses, farmhouses, large estate remnants and mid-century subdivision homes.

Ridgefield sits on bedrock that varies across town. Cameron's Line, a fault formed some 250 million years ago, runs across the southern half, and light earthquakes are occasionally felt along it. North of the line the ground is rich in limestone, which was mined and burned in kilns in the nineteenth century.
